newsitem.title: TURKEY: Resignations batter troubled Turkish coalition.
newsitem.headline: Resignations batter troubled Turkish coalition.

text.p: Two conservative Turkish ministers on Saturday announced their resignations, dealing a blow to the Islamist-led coalition hours before a showdown with secularist army chiefs over the role of Islam in public life.
An aide to Health Minister Yildirim Aktuna told Reuters: "He will hand in his resignation to the prime minister shortly."
Earlier, state-run Anatolian news agency quoted Trade and Industry Minister Yalim Erez as saying he would quit the 10-month-old alliance amid the growing row.

"Out of respect for myself and the Turkish people I will give my resignation to the prime minister," he said after 30 minutes of talks with Tansu Ciller, deputy prime minister and leader of his True Path Party.
The two ministers had publicly denounced Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, for failing to implement demands from the army for a crackdown on religious activism.
The announcements turned up the heat on the coalition, already showing signs of wilting in front of a political onslaught led by the staunchly secularist army brass.

The armed forces, easily the country's most respected institution, have ousted three governments since 1960 but are reluctant to stage another coup for fear of damaging a bid by NATO member Turkey to get closer to Europe.
Leading a charge by Turkey's traditional elites, the military have demanded a broad crackdown on what they see as the creeping Islamisation of life under Erbakan.

Their demands, outlined two months ago but so far largely ignored by Erbakan, are expected to be the focus of Saturday's session of the National Security Council (NSC), where top force commanders have a majority of votes.
The commanders said they had prepared dossiers for the Council on alleged anti-secularist activities, designed to bolster their case against the Islamists.

"We will give the reports. It is up to the council members to make the assessment themselves," NSC general secretary Ilhan Kilic told reporters when asked about the agenda for the meeting, scheduled to begin at 3 p.m. (1200 GMT).
Earlier, armed forces chief Ismail Hakki Karadayi, who sits on the council, served notice the politicians were expected to resolve the crisis -- and soon.

"There are some developments in our country against the basic constitutional properties of our republic to which our people and our armed forces are extremely sensitive," Karadayi told the Anatolian agency.
"Nobody can remain...impartial in the face of this. But the place to resolve this is parliament."

Top of the generals' list of 18 anti-Islamist demands is a call for educational reform that would require students to attend eight years of secular schooling -- rather than the current five years -- before electing optional Koranic training.
Other elements include enforcement of existing bans on traditional Islamic dress, limits on anti-secularist media and restrictions on the secretive Moslem orders.

Erbakan's Welfare Party, which draws many of its cadres from the religious schools, is particularly opposed to the education reform, fearing a sharp downturn in enrolment in these "imam hatip" institutions.
But many in the coalition's junior partner True Path, including U.S.-educated technocrat Ciller who was Turkey's first woman prime minister, back increased mandatory schooling.
The two partners held more than two hours of talks on Friday but were unable break the impasse. They left the meeting separately, without speaking to waiting reporters.
